rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anecdote says a reciter returned an evil eye upon its caster; the caster’s eyes burst while the camel that had fallen ill survived.
rows.anchor: فاخبر الساحي فوقف عليها فقال : حبس حابس وشهاب قابس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report singles out the evil eye and venomous sting as especially suitable for ruqyah; al-Alusi says this means most useful, not exclusive, since the Prophet treated other conditions too.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء في بعضها أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : لارقية الامن عين أو حمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports attest that ruqyah for the evil eye is beneficial and legally prescribed.
rows.anchor: ويدل على نفع الرقية من العين مشروعيتها كما تدل عليه الآثار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anyone who knows he can cast an evil eye should avoid admiring looks and remember God at something pleasing; experienced people say this prevents harm.
rows.anchor: ينبغي لمن علم من نفسه أنه ذو عين أن لاينظر إلى شيء نظر اعجاب

rows.speaker: الأجهوري
rows.claim: Al-Ajhuri recommends blessing the envied person and saying that whatever God wills occurs and strength is only through God.
rows.anchor: ونقل الاجهوري أنه يندب أنه يعوذ المعين فيقول اللهم بارك فيه

rows.speaker: تحفة المحتاج
rows.claim: Tuhfat al-Muhtaj lists the envier’s ablution and prayer for the afflicted person; the afflicted person should also recite the stated formula of divine protection.
rows.anchor: وفي تحفة المحتاج أن من أدويتها أي العين المجربة التي أمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بها

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi recommends that a person who sees himself healthy and in ordinary condition say the protective remembrance.
rows.anchor: ويسن عند القاضي لمن رأى نفسه سليمة واحواله معتدلة أني قول ذلك

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: Scholars quoted in Sharh Muslim say rulers should keep a known envier from mixing with people and support him publicly if poor, because his harm exceeds a leper’s.
rows.anchor: وفي شرح مسلم عن العلماء أنه على السلطان منع من عرف بذلك من مخالطة الناس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says there is no expiation for an envier because the eye is not ordinarily lethal and acts by presence, unlike sorcery.
rows.anchor: وأنه لا كفارة على عائن قيل : لأن العين لاتعد مهلكا عادة

rows.speaker: المالكية
rows.claim: The Malikis reportedly equate the envier with the sorcerer: both are killed if their act kills; other jurists say a sorcerer who admits usually lethal sorcery is killed.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن المالكية أنه لافرق بين الساحر والعائن فيقتلان إذا قتلا

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi reportedly says the evil eye does not affect a noble soul; a report in Ahmad’s Musnad supports the claim.
rows.anchor: ثم إن العين على ما نقل عن الرازي لا تؤثر ممن له نفس شريفة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: A report says a prophet’s admiration of his numerous people caused one hundred thousand deaths overnight; God told him he should have protected them and taught him a prayer.
rows.anchor: واعترض بما رواه القاضي أن نبيا استكثر قومه فمات منهم في ليلة مائة الف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If that report is sound, al-Alusi explains the prophet’s lapse as forgetting remembrance when admiring them, rather than deliberately envying them.
rows.anchor: بأن ذلك النبي عليه السلام لما غفل عن الذكر عند الاستكثار عوتب فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob adds the command to enter by separate gates because avoiding one gate does not itself require separate entrances; the added command stresses his concern.
rows.anchor: لأن عدم الدخول من باب واحد غير مستلزم للدخول من أبواب متفرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob says his planning cannot protect them from anything God decrees; he does not abolish caution, since ordinary means work only by God’s leave and using them is seeking God’s aid.
rows.anchor: أي لاأنفعكم ولا أدفع عنكم بتدبيري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone rules without partner or resistance, and Jacob relies on Him in all that he does or leaves; arranging means does not undermine reliance, as the report says to tie the camel and trust.
rows.anchor: إن الحكم ( أي ما الحكم مطلقا ( إلا لله ( لايشاركه أحد ولا يمانعه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final phrase addresses those who seek to practice reliance on God; Jacob’s sons are especially included and are guided to trust God rather than depend on their father’s precautions.
rows.anchor: أي المريدون للتوكل قيل : جمع بين الواو والفاء في عطف الجملة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One analysis says the fronted phrase restricts reliance to God, the waw coordinates Jacob’s reliance with the command, and the fa makes the prophet’s example a cause for followers’ imitation.
rows.anchor: مع تقديم الصلة للاختصاص ليفيد بالواو عطف فعل غيره من تخصيص التوكل بالله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another analysis calls the fa extra but still causative: using fa alone would express caused exclusivity, not the original point, which is that reliance itself belongs to God.
rows.anchor: ولا بد من القول بزيادة الفاء وإفادتها السببية ويلتزم أن الزائد قد يدل على معنى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some prefer treating the fa as emphasis alone, the common function of extra particles; al-Alusi notes that the grammatical proposals remain debatable.
rows.anchor: واختار بعضهم أنه جيء بالفاء افادة للتأكيد فقط كما هو الأمر الشائع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The brothers entered through separate gates of the city, reportedly four; mentioning their obedience also conveys that they refrained from the single gate Jacob forbade.
rows.anchor: من الأبواب المتفرقة من البلد قيل : كانت له أربعة أبواب فدخلوا منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The entry did not avert what God decreed; the past and imperfect forms indicate its inability to help became actual when harm arrived, though it was already no future safeguard at entry.
rows.anchor: والجملة قيل : جواب ( لما ) والجمع بين صيغتي الماضي والمستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The point is that entry did not cause the failure of protection, unlike the warning that increased people’s aversion; it failed to produce the hoped-for benefit.
rows.anchor: بل بيان عدم سببيته للاغناء مع كونها متوقعة في بادئ الرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, since Jacob had said his measures could not avert God’s decree, the verse narrates the expected outcome: they obeyed but still met the feared event.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قيل : ولما فعلوا ما وصاهم به لم يفدهم ذلك شيئا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan takes the negative clause as the answer to لما, supporting the view that لما is a conditional particle of necessary consequence rather than a time adverb.
rows.anchor: والى كون الجواب ماذكر ذهب أبو حيان وقال : إن فيه حجة لمن زعم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Those treating لما as a time adverb can instead make يوسف’s receiving them its answer, or posit an omitted answer such as their compliance; Ibn Atiyya adopts the omitted-answer analysis.
rows.anchor: والثاني أنه محذوف أي امتثلوا أو قضوا حاجة أبيهم وإلى الوجه الأخير ذهب ابن عطية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An objection says the brothers did avert the specific evil eye by entering separately, so saying that no benefit resulted seems mistaken.
rows.anchor: واعترض القول بعدم ترتب الغرض على التدبير بأن الغرض ليس الا دفع اصابة العين لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reply takes the intended protection broadly; another calamity befell them despite avoiding the eye, and their humiliation and their father’s compounded grief made the precaution seem fruitless.
rows.anchor: واستظهر أن المراد أنه عليه السلام خشى عليهم شر العين فأصابهم شر أخر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the evil eye itself struck them, so the precaution achieved nothing; al-Alusi calls that explanation strained.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن ماأصابهم من العين أيضا فلم يترتب الغرض على التدبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A grammatical objection says the perfect-imperfect pairing usually expresses continuity, which seems not to fit; reading it as denying continuous benefit or continuous non-benefit remains uncertain.
rows.anchor: واعترض أيضا ماذكر في توجيه الجمع بين صيغتي الماضي والمستقبل بأن المشهور

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi offers two parses for the extra من: it may accompany the accusative object or be extra with the nominative subject; the latter removes a pronoun referring to the entry.
rows.anchor: هذا وما أشرنا اليه من زيادة ( من ) في المنصوب هو أحد وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is disconnected: Jacob fulfilled his need to voice concern and caution, not because he believed planning changes destiny; his need was compassion and fear they would be envied.
rows.anchor: إلا حاجة ( استثناء منقطع أي ولكن حاجة ( في نفس يعقوب قضاها

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines need as dependence on something joined with love and lists حاج, حاجات, and حوائج as plurals; an unnamed critic denies حوائج, but eloquent usage refutes him.
rows.anchor: وذكر الراغب أن الحاجة إلى الشيء الفقر اليه مع محبته وجمعه حاج وحاجات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming Jacob explicitly conveys tenderness, compassion, and mercy, fitting his well-known grief and emotional delicacy.
rows.anchor: وفي التصريح باسمه عليه السلام إشعار بالتعطف والشفقة والترحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse returns قضاها to the brothers’ entry: it fulfilled Jacob’s wish that they enter separately; the exception remains disconnected and the clause describes the need.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون ضمير ( قضاها ) للدخول على معنى أن ذلك الدخول قضى حاجة

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: A grammatical proposal treats إلا as لكن, with the following phrase as its subject and predicate; al-Alusi rejects this because Arabic grammarians do not assign إلا that syntax.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن عمل إلا بمعنى لكن عملها مما لم يقل به أحد من أهل العربية

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi allows a connected exception, like the cited poetic construction: the only benefit was Jacob’s compassion, powerless against divine decree, so nothing truly helped them.
rows.anchor: وجوز الطيبى كون الاستثناء متصلا على أنه من باب + ولا عيب فيهم غير أن سيوفهم +

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred reading takes Jacob’s knowledge as a gift through revelation and evidence, since he knew caution did not alter destiny; the causal lam and مصدرية ما support this.
rows.anchor: وإنه لذو علم ( جليل ( لما علمناه ( أي لتعليمنا إياه بالوحي

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aعمash’s reading مما علمناه supports interpreting ما as a verbal noun and the lam as causal.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد التعليل قراءة الأعمش ( مما علمناه )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ما may be a relative pronoun and the phrase praise Jacob’s preservation and watchfulness regarding what God taught him; another gloss says he understood its benefits and acted on it.
rows.anchor: وجوز كون ( ما ) موصولا اسميا والضمير لها واللام صلة علم والمراد به الحفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic إن and lam, indefinite علم, and attribution of teaching to the divine plural magnify Jacob’s rank and knowledge.
rows.anchor: وفي تأكيد الجملة بان واللام وتنكير ( علم ) وتعليله بالتعليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people fail to know the secret of destiny and suppose caution can overcome it; this is the preferred referent of the closing clause.
rows.anchor: سر القدر ويزعمون أنه يغني عنه الحذر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another gloss says people do not know that caution is obligatory though it cannot change destiny; al-Alusi rejects this because the context concerns a failed expected outcome.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد ( لايعلمون ) إيجاب الحذر مع أنه لاينبغي شيئا من القدر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further gloss takes the people to be polytheists who do not know Jacob’s exceptional learning and God’s guidance of His friends; al-Alusi says this is remote from the passage.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد ( لايعلمون ) أن يعقوب عليه السلام بهذه المثابة من العلم

rows.speaker: بعض أفاضل المتأخرين
rows.claim: A later Sufi scholar distinguishes decree as God’s universal judgment on immutable entities, destiny as its specification through times and causes, and destiny’s secret as each entity appearing according to fixed preparedness.
rows.anchor: فالقضاء هو الحكم الكلي على أعين الموجودات بأحوال جارية وأحكام طارئة عليها

rows.speaker: بعض أفاضل المتأخرين
rows.claim: This account says the secret of the secret is that primordial preparedness is uncreated; divine knowledge follows entities as they are, and decree and creation follow that knowledge, making deviation impossible.
rows.anchor: وسر سر القدر هو أن تلك الاستعدادات أزلية غير مجعولة بجعل الجاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although caution cannot change destiny, God commands ordinary means to preserve this world’s order; a prophet refusing to seek food was told that without taking means he would not be provided for.
rows.anchor: فلذا يلغو الحذر لكن أمر به رعاية للأسباب فان تعطيلها مما يفوت انتظام أمر

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Another explanation says many outcomes are decreed conditionally on voluntary human acts, so protection may itself depend on caution without contradicting the preceding account.
rows.anchor: إن سبب إيجاب الحذر أن كثيرا من الأمور قضى معلقا ونيط تحصيله بالأفعال الاختيارية

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi describes destiny as a rank between the divine Essence and manifestations, inaccessible in its full reality so creatures cannot share God’s comprehensive knowledge.
rows.anchor: وذكر الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره أن القدر مرتبة بين الذات والمظاهر ومن علم الله تعالى علمه

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Even when a person knows some matter, he cannot know how divine knowledge attaches to it; every matter has a destiny ruling known only to God.
rows.anchor: فان العبد جاهل بكيفية تعلق العلم مطلقا بمعلومه فلا يصح أن يقع الاشتراك

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: The secret is withheld because complete knowledge would make a person independent of God; it will be disclosed only when God becomes their sight.
rows.anchor: ولو علمت أحكامه لاستقل العبد في العلم بكل شيء وما احتاج اليه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports discourage seeking knowledge of destiny; one says God warned Ezra that continued questioning would erase his name from the prophetic register.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أن عزيرا عليه السلام كان كثير السؤال عنه إلى أن قال الحق سبحانه له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Demanding hidden causes for divine acts is misguided: no cause compels God to create, eternity admits no such causal question, and asking reflects ignorance of God.
rows.anchor: فان أفعال الحق لاينبغي أن تعلل فان ما ثم علة موجبة لتكوين شيء

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The brothers present Benjamin as the brother they were ordered to bring; Yusuf welcomes them and receives their father’s greetings and prayer, then weeps on reading his letter, according to Abu Mansur al-Mahrani.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو منصور المهراني : إنه عليه السلام خاطبه بذلك في كتاب فلما قرأه يوسف

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Yusuf hosts and pairs the brothers at meals and for sleep; Benjamin is alone, so Yusuf sits and sleeps with him, embraces him, and asks about his family.
rows.anchor: فبقي بنيامين وحيدا فبكى وقال : لو كان أخي يوسف حيا لأجلسني معه

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: After Benjamin says his ten sons’ names commemorate a lost brother and that no one like Yusuf could replace him, Yusuf cries, embraces him, and reveals his identity.
rows.anchor: ولكن لم يلدك يعقوب ولا راحيل فبكى يوسف عليه السلام وقام اليه وعانقه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن إسحاق وغيرهما
rows.claim: The reported and preferred account says Yusuf disclosed that he was truly Benjamin’s brother; Ibn Ishaq adds that he told him not to worry about the coming stratagem.
rows.anchor: والقول بأنه عليه السلام تعرف اليه وأعلمه بأنه أخوه حقيقة هو الظاهر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya considers it implausible that “what they did” refers to Yusuf’s servants’ later handling of the cup, since that reading poorly fits ordinary speech.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية : وعلى هذا التأويل يحتمل أن يشير ( بما كانوا يعملون )

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says Yusuf only promised to stand in the lost brother’s place in affection and did not reveal his identity at this point.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب : إنما أخبر عليه السلام أنه قائم مقام أخيه الذاهب في الود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not grieve” reassures Benjamin about the brothers’ past jealousy and abuse: God has reunited them well, and Benjamin must keep the disclosure secret.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ( لاتبتئس ) الخ لاتحزن بما كنت تلقاه منهم من الحسد والأذى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Benjamin refused to leave Yusuf; Yusuf explained retaining him would deepen Jacob’s grief, so Benjamin agreed to a plan to hide the cup and accuse him after the brothers departed.
rows.anchor: قال : فاني أدس صاعي في رحلك ثم أنادي عليك بأنك سرقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusuf completed their provisions and, according to a report, gave each brother an extra camel-load.
rows.anchor: ووفى لهم الكيل وزاد كلا منهم على ما روى حمل بعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The siqayah was the king’s drinking vessel and also measured grain; other accounts say it watered animals and measured grain, and scarcity explains using it as the measure.
rows.anchor: جعل السقاية ( هي إناء يشرب به الملك وبه كان يكال الطعام للناس

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The vessel was reportedly silver inlaid with jewels according to Ikrima, plain silver according to Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, gold according to Ibn Zayd, or silver gilded with gold.
rows.anchor: وكانت من فضة مرصعة بالجواهر على ما روى عن عكرمة أو بدون ذلك كما روى عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another description makes it a long vessel like the Persian mukuk used by non-Arabs; a similar cup reportedly belonged to al-Abbas before Islam.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كانت إناء مستطيلة تشبه المكوك الفارسي الذي يلتقي طرفاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording makes Yusuf the one who placed the cup, though his status as king suggests he ordered someone else to do it; Benjamin may or may not have known.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الجاعل هو يوسف عليه السلام نفسه ويظهر من حيث كونه ملكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading adds waw to جعل: Kufans may treat it as extra, or it may coordinate with an omitted answer to لما, such as letting them depart before placing the cup.
rows.anchor: وقرئ ( وجعل ) بواو وفي ذلك احتمالان الأول أن تكون الواو زائدة على مذهب الكوفيين

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: The herald’s cry is glossed as a caller shouting; al-Kashshaf and others say simply that a caller called out.
rows.anchor: ثم أذن مؤذن ( نادى مسمع كما في مجمع البيان وفي الكشاف وغيره نادى مناد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says “a caller called” is pointless; the reply is that the caller is understood as a designated man whose role is to announce the message.
rows.anchor: وأورد عليه أن النحاة قالوا : لايقال قام قائم لأنه لافائدة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿir denotes loaded camels because they travel back and forth; here it means the caravan’s people by metaphor or ellipsis, like addressing God’s horses to ride.
rows.anchor: والعير الإبل التي عليها الأحمال سميت بذلك لأنها تعير أي تذهب وتجيء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another etymology begins with a donkey caravan and extends the word to any caravan; it derives from ʿayr, “donkey,” with vowel changes like bayḍ and ghīd.
rows.anchor: وقيل : العير قافلة الحمير ثم توسع ( 3 ) فيها حتى قيلت لكل قافلة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Most reports identify the caravan as camels, while Mujahid says it consisted of donkeys.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنها كانت قافلة حمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Yusuf ordered the accusation, “thieves” may mean their deceitful taking of him, include Benjamin by generalization, or accuse them of stealing the cup; a lie may be allowed for benefit, while Benjamin’s consent only removes his distress.
rows.anchor: أريد بالسرقة أخذهم له من أبيه على وجه الخيانة كالسراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusation could be a rhetorical question, “Are you thieves?” but al-Alusi finds this distant; absent Yusuf’s order, the caller may have spoken from his own assumption.
rows.anchor: أو يكون المعنى على الاستفهام أي أئنكم لسارقون ولا يخفى مافيه من البعد

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan’s apparent reading is that the plot, accusation, and distress caused to Jacob were inspired by God for a wise purpose, supported by “Thus We planned for Joseph.”
rows.anchor: وفي البحر الذي يظهر أن هذا التحيل ورمى البراء بالسرقة وادخال الهم

rows.speaker: اليماني
rows.claim: Al-Yamani reads إنكم سارقون without the emphatic lām found in the common reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ اليماني ( إنكم سارقون ) بلا لام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They turn toward the people seeking the cup, or the herald if the term means several callers; this circumstantial phrase shows alarm at an accusation contrary to their conduct.
rows.anchor: وأقبلوا عليهم ( أي على طالبي السقاية المفهوم من الكلام أو على المؤذن

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines فقد as losing something that existed, narrower than nonexistence; another gloss says an item went missing without the person causing it, and the present tense makes the scene vivid.
rows.anchor: والفقد كما قال الراغب : عدم الشيء بعد وجوده فهو أخص من العدم

rows.speaker: السلمي
rows.claim: Al-Sulami reads تفقدون with a damma on ta, meaning “do you find it missing?” Abu Hatim weakens it; al-Alusi explains it from أفقدته.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السلمي ( تفقدون ) بضم التاء من أفقدته إذا وجدته فقيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asking what was missing instead of what they stole displays innocence, leaves open accidental loss, teaches courtesy, and avoids rash accusation.
rows.anchor: إرشاد لهم إلى مراعاة حسن الأدب والاحتراز عن المجازفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They answer that the king’s cup is missing rather than immediately denying theft; one explanation is that they first complete the allegation so any defect can end the dispute.
rows.anchor: ولم يقولوا سرقتموه أو سرق وقيل : كان الظاهر أن يبادروا بالانكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-suwaʿ is the measuring vessel, the siqayah itself; naming the king’s cup clarifies the allegation, and the repeated verb or present tense follows earlier wording or creates verbal matching.
rows.anchor: والصواع بوزن غراب المكيال وهو السقاية ولم يعبر بها مبالغة في الافهام

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو حيوة وابن جبير
rows.claim: One set of readings keeps the common form but pronounces ṣad with kasra; Abu Hurayra and Mujahid read صاع, Abu Raja صوع, and Ibn Awn صوع with damma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو حيوة وابن جبير فيما نقل ابن عطية كما قرأ الجمهور إلا أنهم كسروا الصاد

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن جبير ويحيى بن يعمر وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: Other readings are صواغ, its shortened form with a silent waw, and صوغ as a verbal noun used for the crafted object; all are variants of the measure’s name.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن جبير فيما نقل عنهما صاحب اللوامح ( صواغ ) بالغين المعجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vessel name may be masculine or feminine, though Abu Ubayda did not attest feminine usage; حمل with kasra is detached cargo and with fatha attached cargo, following al-Raghib’s distinction.
rows.anchor: وهو مما يذكر ويؤنث وأبو عبيدة لم يحفظ التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever brings it” may mean anyone who produces it, even himself, or one who identifies and exposes the thief; the reward is a camel-load of food.
rows.anchor: ولمن جاء به ( أي أتى به مطلقا ولو من عند نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caller is guarantor for the promised payment; this supports making surety conditional on the event creating the obligation, and prior peoples’ law applies when not repudiated.
rows.anchor: أي كفيل أؤديه اليه وهو قول المؤذن + واستدل بذلك كما في الهداية

rows.speaker: بعض الشافعية
rows.claim: Some Shafiʿis object that the verse concerns a reward contract, not surety, because the caller guarantees his own payment; they also say the beneficiary is unspecified.
rows.anchor: الأول ماقاله بعض الشافعية من أن هذه الآية محمولة على الجعالة لما يأتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reply takes زعيم in its true sense: the caller relays the king’s promise and guarantees it on the king’s behalf, so it is genuine surety; invalidity of one combined commitment does not void the other.
rows.anchor: بأن الزعم حقيقة في الكفالة والعمل بها مهما أمكن واجب

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
rows.claim: A report glosses زعيم as guarantor, but al-Ahkam says this is not personal surety: the caller guarantees the finder’s reward, establishing a reward or hire contract for an open task.
rows.anchor: وفي كتاب الأحكام أنه روى عن عطاء الخراساني ( زعيم ) بمعنى كفيل

rows.speaker: محمد بن الحسن
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan says the camel-load may have been a known amount, resolving the objection that hire requires specified compensation.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال محمد بن الحسن في السير الكبير : ولعل حمل البعير كان قدرا معلوما

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam says their law accepted surety and the prophetic rule says a guarantor is liable; the load was known, though it secured return of stolen property before a debt was due.
rows.anchor: وقال الامام : إن الآية تدل على أن الكفالة كانت صحيحة في شرعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their law may have accepted this surety, but there is no evidence that the person returning the cup was known to be its thief, so that legal premise need not be assumed.
rows.anchor: ولعل مثل هذه الكفالة كانت تصح عندهم وتعقب بأنه لادليل على أن الراد

rows.speaker: أكثر النحويين
rows.claim: Most grammarians say oath-ta replaces waw, as in تراث and توراة; others derive it from ba, while al-Suhayli calls it original.
rows.anchor: أكثر النحويين على أن التاء بدل من الواو كما أبدلت في تراث وتوراة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ta is used for oaths only with God; al-Alusi objects that it also precedes Lord, the Kaaba, al-Rahman, and other expressions.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : إنها لايقسم بها إلا في الله خاصة وتعقب بالمنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever its etymology, the oath conveys astonishment at being accused despite their known conduct; they reportedly muzzled their camels and were known in Egypt for piety and decency.
rows.anchor: وأياما كان ففي القسم بها معنى التعجب كأنهم تعجبوا من رميهم بما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You know” means certain knowledge matching reality; “we did not come to corrupt the land” means they came neither to steal nor to commit other corruption.
rows.anchor: علما جاز ما مطابقا للواقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation construes their denial as denying corrupt intent even if an accidental act occurred; another says they deny even imagining corruption, which al-Alusi finds remote.
rows.anchor: ونفي المجيء للإفساد وإن لم يكن مستلزما لما هو مقتضى المقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We were never thieves” describes their established character; the audience’s knowledge of their past follows from observing them, and knowledge is invoked as witness and emphasis.
rows.anchor: أي ما كنا نوصف بالسرقة قط والظاهر دخول هذا في حيز العلم كالأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can use “you know” like an oath, as in the cited poem, binding the hearers and reinforcing the brothers’ astonishment.
rows.anchor: ولذا أجرت العرب العلم مجرى القسم كما في قوله : ولقد علمت لتأتين منيتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic continuation says death’s arrows never miss, illustrating how a knowledge-clause can function like an oath and bind its hearers.
rows.anchor: إن المنايا لاتطيش سهامها وفي ذلك من إلزام الحجة عليهم وتحقيق أمر التعجب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some allow “we did not come to corrupt” to be the object of “you know,” the oath’s answer, or the answer to knowledge because knowledge implies it; this does not exclude the prior analysis.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أنه يجوز أن يكون كما جئنا الخ متعلق العلم وأن يكون جواب القسم

rows.speaker: أصحاب يوسف
rows.claim: Joseph’s attendants ask what punishment applies to the cup or its theft under the brothers’ law if their claim of innocence is false; the omitted possessive links punishment to crime, or figuratively to the thief.
rows.anchor: قالوا ( أي أصحاب يوسف عليه السلام ( فما جزاؤه ( أي الصواع والكلام على حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: الإخوة
rows.claim: The brothers say whoever has the cup found in his baggage is to be enslaved; their wording avoids calling anyone a thief because their law enslaves thieves, not accidental possessors.
rows.anchor: واختاروا عنوان الوجدان في الرحل دون السرقة مع أنه المراد لأن كون الأخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They repeat “that is his penalty” to affirm both the ruling and its rightful application; the fa presents the conclusion as following from their accepted rule, so it is not empty repetition.
rows.anchor: فالغرض من الأول إفادة الحكم ومن الثاني إفادة حقيته والاحتفاظ بشأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically من can be a relative or conditional subject, with following clauses as predicate; an objection says the embedded sentence lacks a pronoun linking it back.
rows.anchor: وجوز كون ( من ) موصولة مبتدأ وهذه الجملة خبره والفاء لتضمن المبتدأ معنى الشرط

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The reply is that repeated الجزاء can stand where a pronoun would, with the original sense “it is the penalty”; explicit repetition clarifies and magnifies the ruling.
rows.anchor: والربط كما يكون بالضمير يكون بالظاهر والأصل جزاؤه من وجد في رحله فهو هو

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: A poetic line about death defeating rich and poor supports using the explicit repeated noun for cohesion, answering the objection that overt nouns replace pronouns only for honorific emphasis.
rows.anchor: نغص الموت ذا الغنى والفقيرا وبذلك يندفع ما في البحر اعتراضا على هذا الجعل

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that reporting “its penalty is this” adds little after the question; the reply says it assures the questioner the ruling is understood and encourages acceptance.
rows.anchor: وتعقب ذلك أبو حيان بأنه ليس في الاخبار عن المسؤول عنه بذلك كثير فائدة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another says the wording is a rhetorical, disbelieving question before giving the obvious answer; al-Alusi dismisses this as implausible.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن الجملة من الخبر والمبتدأ المحذوف على معنى الاستفهام الانكاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing “Thus we punish wrongdoers” most naturally remains the brothers’ speech, reaffirming the penalty and condemning theft; they are confident of innocence and unaware of the trap.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا من تتمة كلام الاخوة فهو تأكيد للحكم المذكور غب تأكيد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other attributions make the closing words Joseph’s attendants’ speech or Joseph’s, meaning they punish thieves with the penalty just described.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو من كلام أصحاب يوسف عليه السلام وقيل : كلامه نفسه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say the herald searched the baggage because he was mentioned immediately before; another says Yusuf did it, as reports place the search after the brothers returned from a stop or town outskirts.
rows.anchor: قيل المؤذن ورجح بقرب سبق ذكره وقيل : يوسف عليه السلام فقد روى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Yusuf speaks with the brothers, the search likely followed their return, though attributing it to Yusuf is metonymic: his attendants physically searched at his command.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن الظاهر أن إسناد التفتيش اليه عليه السلام مجازي والمفتش حقيقة أصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Yusuf first remarked that Benjamin probably took nothing; the brothers insisted he inspect the baggage for their peace of mind, and he agreed.
rows.anchor: قال : ماأظن هذا أخذ شيئا فقالوا : والله لا تتركه حتى تنظر في رحله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “then he extracted it” can refer to the cup, which is masculine or feminine, or to the theft understood from context; the wording clarifies the source and owner.
rows.anchor: أي السقاية أو الصواع لأنه كما علمت مما يؤنث ويذكر عند الحفاظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وعاء means a container and may include baggage and other receptacles, fitting a search of everything they carried better than the narrower رحال.
rows.anchor: والوعاء الظرف الذي يحفظ فيه الشيء وكأن المراد به هنا ما يشمل الرحل وغيره

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم السمرقندي
rows.claim: Matching plural and singular forms does not require one-to-one pairing: each may ride one mount, but each may sell a different number, so the brother’s vessel may be singular or plural.
rows.anchor: كما قال المدقق أبو القاسم السمرقندي لايقتضي أن يلزم في كل مقابلة مقارنة الواحد

rows.speaker: الحسن ونافع
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, also reported from Nafi, reads وعاء with damma on waw; Ibn Jubayr reads إعاء with an initial hamza, a regular change for initial kasra-waw in Hudhayl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ( وعاء ) بضم الواو وجاء كذلك عن نافع وقرأ ابن جبير ( إعاء )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s plan guided the brothers, through questions from attendants, to state the penalty Yusuf needed without realizing they were enabling his aim.
rows.anchor: أي مثل ذلك الكيد العجيب وهو إرشاد الأخوة إلى الافتاء المذكور بأجرائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here كدنا means arranging steps toward Yusuf’s purpose, including hiding the cup; “plotting” is metaphorical because literal deception is impossible for God.
rows.anchor: أي صنعنا ودبرنا لأجل تحصيل غرضه من المقدمات التي رتبها من دس السقاية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other accounts treat the wording as representation or as two attributions, implicitly to Yusuf literally and explicitly to God metaphorically; al-Alusi says the latter is weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن ذلك محمول على التمثيل وقيل : إن في الكيد اسنادين بالفحوى

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtada says كدنا means “we intended,” citing a poem.
rows.anchor: وفي درر المرتضى ان كدنا بمعنى أردنا وأنشد

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtada’s poem supports reading كدنا as “we intended.”
rows.anchor: كادت وكدت وتلك خير ارادة لو عاد من لهو الصبابة ما مضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in ليوسف marks benefit, unlike the harm-oriented lām in the earlier plot against Joseph.
rows.anchor: واللام للنفع لا كاللام في قوله تعالى : ( فيكيدوا لك كيدا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: في دين الملك may mean the king’s authority, according to Ibn Abbas, or his law and judgment, according to Qatada.
rows.anchor: أي في سلطانه على ما روى عن ابن عباس أو في حكمه وقضائه كما روى عن قتادة

rows.speaker: الكلبي وغيره
rows.claim: The scheme was needed because the king’s law punished theft by doubled compensation and beating, not by taking the accused as a slave under Jacob’s law.
rows.anchor: لأن جزاء السارق في دينه على ما روى عن الكلبي وغيره أن يضاعف عليه العزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Unless God wills” may refer to His will embodied in the plot or His willing Yusuf’s taking Benjamin this way; the broader account includes all the guided actions and required steps.
rows.anchor: إلا حال مشيئته تعالى التي هي عبارة عن ذلك الكيد أو إلا حال مشيئته تعالى للأخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes the clause explain the plot by saying God willed the king’s law to permit this judgment, though al-Alusi notes a problem; a disconnected exception means God permitted taking him under another law.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن جملة ما كان الخ في موضع البيان والتفسير للكيد وأن معنى الاستثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: نرفع درجات means raising lofty ranks of knowledge; its case may be adverbial, governed by an omitted preposition, or cognate accusative, while من نشاء is the object.
rows.anchor: أي رتبا كثيرة عالية من العلم وانتصابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperfect verb presents raising as a continuing divine practice, and “above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing” marks higher knowledge.
rows.anchor: وإيثار صيغة الاستقبال للاشعار بأن ذلك سنة مستمرة غير مختصة بهذه المادة

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: If the plot means steering the brothers to issue the ruling, Joseph’s elevation is his skill as a necessary part of securing Benjamin; if it means instruction, it includes teaching the needed ruling.
rows.anchor: إنه إن جعل الكيد عبارة عن إرشاد الاخوة إلى الافتاء وحملهم عليه

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: On the first reading, “above every knower” explains that Joseph’s rank alone could not secure the plan, since he did not know whether his brothers would comply; God guided them too.
rows.anchor: بل إنما نرفع كل من نرفع حسب استعداد وفوق كل واحد منهم عليم

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: On the teaching reading, God taught Yusuf through the verdict his brothers would give; this praises Yusuf’s high learning and connects the raised ranks to the divine plan.
rows.anchor: وحينئذ يكون قوله تعالى : ( نرفع ) إلى ( عليم ) توضيحا لذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says every scholar stands above another until knowledge reaches God; Yusuf’s brothers were learned, but Yusuf surpassed them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما : فوق كل عالم عالم إلى أن ينتهي العلم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the closing phrase either distributively, with a scholar above each knower, or as God above all scholars; both readings explain the conclusion.
rows.anchor: وفوق كل ذي علم عليم فوقه أرفع درجة منه في علمه أو فوق العلماء كلهم عليم

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf explains that the first reading praises Yusuf for surpassing learned brothers, while the second affirms God alone raises whom He wills; the indefinite after كل supports distributive reading.
rows.anchor: أن غرضه أن يبين وجه التذييل بهذه الجملة فأفاد أنه إما على وجه التأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion distinguishes knowledge considered without limit from individual knowers: one reading ascends through higher knowledge without end, the other compares each knower with another.
rows.anchor: لو نظر إلى العلم ولا تناهيه كان الأول فيرتقي إلى مالا نهاية لعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers taking the first clause as praising Yusuf and magnifying the divine plan, and the second as a humbling reminder of God’s superior knowledge.
rows.anchor: ولعل اعتبار كون الجملة الأولى مدحا ليوسف عليه السلام وتعظيما لشأن الكيد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some use the verse to argue that God knows by His essence rather than an added attribute: otherwise a knower would have to stand above Him.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل بالآية من ذهب إلى أنه تعالى شأنه عالم بذاته لا بصفة علم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply restricts “every possessor of knowledge” to created beings, since the context concerns creation, and reads العليم as God, more knowledgeable than every creature.
rows.anchor: بأن المراد بكل ذي علم المخلوقات ذوو العلم لأن الكلام في الخلق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Said ibn Jubayr says Ibn Abbas rebuked a man’s recitation and declared God the Knower, above every scholar; al-Dahhak likewise says the verse means God Himself.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس : بئسما قلت الله العليم وهو فوق كل عالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the opposing proof would imply God is not a knower if it also accepts “above all scholars is a knower,” so its argument fails by its own logic.
rows.anchor: على أنه لو صح ماذكره المستدل لم يكن الله تعالى عالما

rows.speaker: غير واحد من السبعة
rows.claim: Most read درجات من نشاء without annexation; another reading annexes درجات to من نشاء, which some say better matches the following mention of God’s supremacy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ غير واحد من السبعة ( درجات من نشاء ) بالأضافة قيل : والقراءة الأولى

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaqub reads يرفع and يشاء in third-person singular; Isa of Basra reads نرفع, indefinite درجات, then من يشاء, a reading al-Lawāmi calls less favored but not rejectable.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب بالياء في ( يرفع ) و ( يشاء ) وقرأ عيسى البصرة

rows.speaker: عبدالله الحبر
rows.claim: Abdullah al-Hibr is reported to read “above every ذي عالم”; explanations treat ذي as extra, عالم as a verbal noun, or an omitted person; another report omits ذي and is called likelier.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبدالله الحبر ( وفوق كل ذي عالم عليم ) فخرجت كما في البحر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid’s report says Yusuf’s aunt, who inherited Isaac’s belt and loved him dearly, hid it under his clothes and accused him; finding it let her keep him until her death.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج ابن إسحاق وابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم عن مجاهد قال : كان أول مادخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ claim that Benjamin steals refers to Yusuf, whom they say stole the belt from his aunt before; the cited story explains their allegation.
rows.anchor: إن يسرق ( يعنون بنيامين ( فقد سرق أخ له من قبل ( يريدون به يوسف
